utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Although there are a few leftovers from the MFI list of last week, I think we'd better start with the witness now and see whether we can deal with those leftovers later. Mr. Kay, is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. And thank you for the indication concerning the housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we call Mr. Radin, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radin. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. I see that the text has already been handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radin. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, just to make things clear, you speak English, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you would prefer to give your evidence in your own language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, could you look at a document that will be put in front of you on the screen there, 2D00718. On the right-hand screen.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see a document there in your own language?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I think this is the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And is this document signed by you?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you sign the end of the document and the pages in between?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I signed the document at the end, and I believe I initialed all of the pages between the first and last.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the information in that document, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Reading the document subsequently, I found a typographical error. There was a simple mistake in letter pertaining to Ms. Skare Ozbolt, who was the then Assistant Minister, as well as Mr. Sarinic, who was not the chef de cabinet in 1995 but sometime previous to that. It must have been in early 1995 that he was appointed chef de cabinet. In essence, the meaning of the sentence does not change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the only two corrections --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to slow down because you develop a speed of speech which the interpreters and transcriber could not follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think what you're referring to is the information contained within paragraph -- I thought 15 but I might be wrong about that. Paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could turn to the second page -- third page of the statement where paragraph 7 is to be found. Oh, the next page - my apologies - in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this the paragraph you were referring to, Mr. Radin, in relation to which you said there was a typographical error concerning Mrs. Skare Ozbolt?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes. In line 13. It says in Croatian "pomicnica." The correction version is "pomocnica." In any case, it is just a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hope that that clears matters up. With Your Honour's leave, is the Court satisfied with that explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that if it's just a typographical error that it has no impact on the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- just -- not on this issue, but I note that the version that I see on the screen seems to be different from the one that was filed, in that there was a typographical error or, rather, an error at the beginning of paragraph 6 where it says on the document on the screen: "In July 1995." What was filed at page 26483 of the written record is: "In September 1995." I had flagged that because it obviously is a mistake from the context, but I'm just wondering if there were any other changes that were made to this document when it was uploaded that would be different from the version we received in the 92 ter filing from the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it looks that the uploaded document is not -- the beginning of paragraph 6 is not the same as the one that was filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see "In July 1995" at the start of paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The version filed started, "In September 1995," which comes as a bit of a surprise, as a matter of fact, but -- so, therefore, July seems to a bit more logical but the filed version says, "In September 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was that alteration which I believe took place in the English language version which was noted as being a typographical error, and that correction was -- was made. I hope that that explains matters. I'm told that that was the only typographical error that was noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this is now clearly on the record. Then I take it that the uploaded version will be the one -- the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, if I were to ask you those questions that you were asked when you made this statement, would you give the same answers today as you gave when you were asked the questions originally?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, in entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, I move that this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1678.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. I have no further questions to ask Mr. Radin, but in according with the practice, I will give a brief summary of the essence of his statement for the record and for those who are listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the 30th of January, 1995, Mr. Radin was appointed as the chef de cabinet of the president of the Republic of Croatia and remained in that position until the 30th of January 2000. At that time in 1995, Mr. Sarinic was the head of the president's office. As the chef de cabinet for the president, Mr. Radin was in charge of the organisational unit in the office of the president. As the president's chef de cabinet, he was formally subordinated to the head of the office, Mr. Sarinic, and he was his immediate superior manager, in terms of organisation. But in carrying out his duties, Mr. Radin was responsible to the president, President Tudjman. His office was located next to the president's office. As the chef de cabinet, he managed the secretaries, the president's archives, and the recording and production of transcripts. On the 1st of August, 1995, the office of the president called Mr. Radin whilst he was on holiday and told him to go to work, not in Brioni where the president happened to be at that time, but to Zagreb. After that conversation, he immediately travelled to Zagreb. On the next day, which was the 2nd of August, 1995, President Tudjman returned from Brioni to Zagreb, and he ordered Mr. Radin to start preparing a reserve location in a place called Tuskanac, a separate place from the presidential palace, and it was from there that the office had to relocate and was located at the time when Operation Oluja was launched. On the 4th of August, at about 5.00 in the morning, Mr. Radin moved with the president to Tuskanac. During the course of the day, the president received various operational reports on the progress of the operation from Minister Susak. At some point on the 4th of August, the president asked Mr. Radin to find Ivan Cermak. He said he would like to send Mr. Cermak as civilian commander of Knin town immediately after the liberation. As far as Mr. Radin can recall today, he asked the president what a civilian commander meant, and he told him that it would be a military person, tasked with establishing normal civilian life as soon as possible and collaborating with civilian authorities in that process. Mr. Radin says that he, in collaboration with the military office, could not find legal grounds for appointing Mr. Cermak as a civilian manager. He contacted the president's military office, asking them to find an appropriate establishment position. The military office drafted and sent for the president's signature, the decree on the appointment of Mr. Cermak as commander of the Knin garrison. On the next day, the 5th of August, Mr. Cermak was found, and he went to Tuskanac. According to Mr. Radin's knowledge, as garrison commander, Mr. Cermak did not have authority to command the civilian police. The appointment of Mr. Cermak was not that kind that would give him such authority. The military appointment of Mr. Cermak was within the regular military establishment, and in the context of the specific situation, it was also to cover specific civilian requirements. And Mr. Radin also describes that finding a formal way of appointing Mr. Cermak was a great problem, because of the lack of position within the establishment structure, and they had requested guidance and explanation from the president in relation to the task. Your Honour, that concludes my summary of the statement of Mr. Radin, and, as I have already informed the Court, I have no further questions to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please wait there, Mr. Radin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kehoe, will it be you who will cross-examine Mr. Radin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. You may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radin. Mr. Radin, I would like to ask to you just --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a couple of clarifying questions from your statement. And if we go to paragraph 17 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring D1678 back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radin, in this section of your statement you were talking about crimes that were occurring in the Krajina after Operation Storm. And if I can highlight one sentence in paragraph 17, you note that -- after talking about arson and other unfortunate incidents you note, and I quote: "International pressure on Croatia was growing because of these unfortunate incidents." Mr. Radin, as a chef de cabinet, was President Tudjman and the other leaders in the Republic of Croatia sensitive to these comments by the international community?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I think it was a sensitive time, because such international pressures could be felt in the various statements of state officials and in the contacts that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Sarinic had in the course of performing their duties in meeting with, be it the ambassadors of foreign states in Croatia or the various representatives of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, just let me take -- maybe "sensitive" is the wrong word. Were they concerned about criticism by the international community?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: There were concerns because the international pressure was something that caused a position for Croatia in the international community which was not a favourable one. Any person working on a state policy needs to be concerned by that, because what always needs to be taken into account is the view of those who are considered friends of Croatia and those who are not so inclined to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk very indirectly if we may, Mr. Radin, about individuals, as opposed to just individuals in the government generally. Was President Tudjman concerned that Croatia was going to be criticised by the international community because of the crimes that had been taking place in the Krajina after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: According to my knowledge as the chef de cabinet, Mr. Tudjman was concerned. And after each such a meeting or assessment, he would be in a way angered by such developments. Namely, every morning, we had regular briefings, discussing the latest news about Croatia in the Croatian press and in international reports. That is to say, the reports of the various press agencies, such as the AP or Reuters and others. Every morning, I attended this so-called press briefing, or briefing for journalists, when the presidential spokesperson would inform or brief us about the latest reports concerning Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when these criminal -- when these reports were being relayed to President Tudjman and the rest of the members of the government about crimes that the press had observed in the Krajina, did President Tudjman want those crimes stopped?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: It was my understanding that the president wanted to see that stop, and that such events were rubbing the wrong way. Given my position at the time, as the chef de cabinet, I wasn't privy to all of the political discussions the president held with the various officials from his office, as well as governmental representatives, and I don't know what measures and occasions they discussed. I do know, however, and I am positive that such events irritated him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, as the chef de cabinet, I mean, you note - excuse me - in paragraph 18, and when you're talking about a plan to expel Serbs, you note, about halfway down: "Had there been such a plan I would have known about it, given the position I held at the time." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if there had been a plan to permit this crime to take place, you would have known that as well, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I believe that I would have known about that. I spent a lot of time in the office, a number of hours every day, seven days a week, and it's very hard for me to believe that such a major plan, a significant plan that would have involved a lot of people, would have been adopted or passed without me knowing -- not knowing about it, living next door to the president's office, seven days a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the bottom portion of paragraph 18, Mr. Radin, you note that the: "But I know that the RH government, i.e., its ministries, tried to normalise the situation in that area by issuing orders on crime prevention ..." Who issued those orders, which ministries issued those orders?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which ministry that was. However, being familiar with the organisation of the government at the time, I would assume that it was the Ministry of Defence that issued orders within its remit. The Ministry of the Interior obviously worked within its purview, and the government, as the umbrella body charged with the executive power, coordinated all of the activities; whereas the tasks of local administration that were carried out by the municipalities were performed by government commissioners and for Knin that was Mr. Petar Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the issuing of orders on crime prevention, did you ever hear President Tudjman oppose any minister or any ministry giving orders to prevent crime? Did you ever hear President Tudjman oppose such an order to prevent crime?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: No. I never heard President Tudjman opposing any such order. On the contrary, President Tudjman never got directly involved with the work of the government. On several occasions, he presided over the sessions of the government but he never meddled with its decisions or with the documents the government passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions for the witness, which means, Mr. Radin, that you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecution. It is Mr. Hedaraly, counsel for the Prosecution, who will cross-examine you. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radin.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy of your statement with you in your language?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I have it in the back room. I don't have anything on me. If you wish me to do so, I can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there must be a hard copy somewhere around which could be made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's okay. We'll refer to it at some point but not right away, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise, you will have on it on your screen anyhow, Mr. Radin. There's no need to leave the courtroom at this moment, and if there would be a spare copy somewhere and then preferably the one with July rather than September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It -- that's the English one rather than the Croatian. I believe the witness will want the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the -- the Croatian one is about July, yes, that's "srpanj."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have it in my red binder. Maybe somebody can fetch that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a copy for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will -- we will print one, Your Honour, and it will be clean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you will receive one, Mr. Radin. Don't worry. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, have you followed any of the proceedings in this case up to now?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: To be honest, not too much. I'm now involved in something else. As far as I could read in the daily press, I did, but I wouldn't say that was too much on -- on the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Have you reviewed any of the filings in this case? For example, the Prosecution's indictment, or its pre-trial brief, or any other documents?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I read the indictment. I did not read the OTP's pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I think you just mentioned that your knowledge of the proceedings, the trial, was largely based on media reports that you would review; was that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: You asked me whether I followed the proceedings. I said that I didn't, that all I know is through media reports. And when you asked me whether I saw any of the documents pertaining to this trial, and the Prosecutor mentioned some of them, I said very clearly that I read the indictment, and that I did not read the other document that the Prosecutor mentioned, the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Radin. Maybe there's a misunderstanding. Perhaps I have asked the question in a not very precise way. My question was regarding your knowledge of the trial, not the indictment but the actual proceedings. That is largely based on media reports that you reviewed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. I read the indictment and I also spoke to Mr. Cermak's Defence team when I provided my statement. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 of your statement, you state your understanding of the Prosecution's position on a few matters. What is that basis -- what is your basis for that understanding?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Paragraph 18 was created as a result of my conversation with General Cermak's Defence team. When they asked me whether I would testify, since I am a legal professional by trade, I wanted to be informed about the framework of the proceedings and the scope of the indictment. And during the first conversation I was told that there was an indictment, although I had already read in the media about the general outlines of it, but that was the first time when I got privy to the entire indictment and read it from the beginning to the end. And that would be all I -- I actually know about the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to -- to clarify that last answer to make sure I understand. So you read the indictment recently, after having met with the Defence team for General Cermak? Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that wasn't so recently. I believe that it was in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you state your understanding of the Prosecution's position, you've indicated that that was based on your conversation with General Cermak's Defence team. So are the details of the Prosecution's position, as you have indicated in your statement, based on conversations you had with the Defence team of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: What I was told briefly by General Cermak's Defence team was later confirmed when I read the indictment. I have the indictment, together with my statement in the back room. I tried to get very well informed and learn about the indictment. To be absolutely clear, I sat down with Mr. Kay and he gave me the major -- the biggest -- the most important outlines of the indictment within the scope of three minutes, and then I read the indictment very carefully, and I provided my answer contained in paragraph 18, as can you read it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you read the indictment -- so just to understand, you met with Mr. Kay, you read the indictment, and only after that, you prepared your statement? Is that the accurate chain of events?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the accurate chain of events, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radin. I just want to briefly touch upon your -- a topic that has been briefly mentioned here, and your relationship with President Tudjman or at least your professional relationship with President Tudjman. Would it be fair to say that although President Tudjman relied on his close collaborators to advise him, he would be the ultimate decision-maker in terms of important or key, strategic decisions?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: President Tudjman made key, strategic decisions, as he should have, according to the constitution. He did have counsel, advisory body, VONS, the Presidential Council. He very often discussed matters with his collaborators. However, when it came to the matters that the president should be in charge of, he was the chief decision-maker.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it also be fair to say that his decisions were final? And I mean that once he made a decision, no one would really argue with him. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I believe this you can't really put it that way. Because there were decisions that -- that he changed. He would change his opinion before the implementation of the decision started. There were decisions that were changed after the beginning of the implementation if the government or -- and somebody else reported to him about problems with the implementation of a specific decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Radin. I just want to move now to the main topic in your statement, which is the appointment of General Cermak. And in your statement, at paragraph 8, you said that President Tudjman told you that he wanted to send Mr. Cermak to Knin as a "civilian commander," and you then asked President Tudjman what that meant. Mr. Radin, am I correct in saying that the reason you sought clarification from the president is that the term "civilian commander" did not make much sense to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Not only because of that. Military duties and the preparation of military documents in President Tudjman's office was what the military office did. I was the chef de cabinet in charge of civilian duties, as it were. I did not have enough knowledge or experience within the military system to be able to immediately assess whether what the president was saying had any legal grounding or not. I was also surprised by the fact that he mentioned Mr. Cermak's name. That's why I asked him for a clarification. I wanted to be absolutely sure what the president's intention was before further discussions ensued with the military cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But even as a non-military person, the expression "civilian commander" was confusing to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, in a certain way. I can -- if ... maybe can I clarify. All decisions on appointment which were prepared by the military cabinet would have to go through the civilian cabinet and finally would reach president for signature. These decisions enabled me to see the structure and the organisation and what appointments were within the president's authority. And that was my source of knowledge of the military system and organisation, and that's what I based my decisions on as to what was normal and what was some -- somewhat unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radin, if I pause sometimes after your answer it's just because I'm getting the full interpretation, so that's why it takes some time. Now, the response you got from President Tudjman, according to your statement, is that that would be a military person tasked with establishing normal civilian life as soon as possible and collaborating with the civilian authorities in that process. So, Mr. Radin, for President Tudjman, it was important that this task be given to a military person; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I believe so. The president paid a lot of attention to the military system. He understood that the situation in Knin was difficult, that the military operation at that moment was drawing to an end, and he wanted to appoint a person in uniform. However, the most important thing was to establish normal life in the shortest possible life [as interpreted]. He wanted the area to have electricity, water, and everything else that a normal civilian life entails. A uniformed person, and I'm talking about my assumptions here, was somebody who would have been aware of the situation on the ground, and he also knew that somebody who wore a uniform and had a high rank would find it much easier to deal with the tasks that he intended to assign to such a person. And that's why I believe the fact that that person wore a uniform seemed so very important to -- to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, in fact, the position of garrison commander is a military position; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is a military position. The position of a -- of garrison commander is a military position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 10 of your statement, you state that there was no real position for Mr. Cermak within the establishment structure, and that later on, that is why he was appointed as a garrison commander. Do you recall that -- making that statement?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I recall that, and if you will allow me, I would like to explain the chain of events. On the 4th, the president asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Your statement is in evidence so you've explained it there. If you want to add something that is not in your statement, then are you welcome to do so, but there is no need to just repeat what is there. I know have you explained it there, and I will you my question. If you feel a need to go back to your explanation, of course, you can free to do so. Is that -- is that okay?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I apologise, I understand and I would kindly ask to you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I haven't asked you my question yet but I will -- I will now. Let me first show you on the screen 65 ter 2D00-0627. And what will you see on the screen, Mr. Radin, is a decision from President Tudjman on the basis and organisation of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to the second page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You will see a number of positions created. Now, I don't want to go through these in detail. But if I could just move to the last page of the document to show that you the date of that decision is November 1991. Now if we can move in the English back to the previous page and stay on the same page in the B/C/S version, you can see the item under Roman numeral XVII which says: "Other administrations and departments may be formed for the needs of war or in exceptional circumstances?" My question for you, Mr. Radin, is: In light of this, President Tudjman could created a special administration or department for Mr. Cermak in Knin; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I would like to be able to answer your question. However, I'm not very well versed in the military system and organisation. I don't think I ever saw this document. If I did, it was a long time ago. And it would be very difficult for me to provide any explanation based on just one excerpt or one provision of a decree. So with all due respect, I hope you won't mind me saying that I'm not able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. Radin. Thank you for -- thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could tender 65 ter 2D00-0627 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will becomes Exhibit P2639.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And the document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, you were not present at the meeting between Mr. Cermak and President Tudjman on 5 August at Tuskanac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, you were not present; or no, that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I was not present at the meeting. I was in the building where the meeting took place, but I was not at the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it is because it was at Tuskanac and not in the presidential palace at Pantovcak that this meeting was not taped; is that also right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I suppose this is correct, because all the preparations for Tuskanac were done in a bit of a haste, and I suppose that recording had not been provided for -- for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you referred also to a VONS meeting on 5 August 1995 at paragraph 13 of your statement. And would it be fair to say that that meeting was also not taped for the same reason?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes. However, that VONS session was a ceremonious one more than anything else because it was held to celebrate the liberation of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now going back to Mr. Cermak's role in Knin. Now some of the functions given by President Tudjman to General Cermak went beyond those of a regular garrison commander. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: As far as I understood the president's intention, I would say yes. This related to the civilian part of the tasks that had to do with the putting in place conditions for a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, therefore, would it be fair to say that General Cermak, after his appointment, had a dual role. On the one hand, he had the military role as a garrison commander; but also had an additional role as dealing with international organisations, including the United Nations. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Based on my conversation with the president, I did not understand that his chief task was to be communication [as interpreted] with the international organisations. The way I understood things was that Mr. Cermak, as a very skillful businessperson, would be able to secure normal conditions for life in that city. I don't know if Mr. Cermak speaks any foreign language, and I'm sure that the president, if he wanted somebody in that position to be also in charge of contacts with internationals, would have sent to that position somebody with previous diplomatic experience, somebody who spoke foreign languages, but that is only my understanding of the whole situation, my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to my question and rephrase it, in light of your -- of your comment. So would you agree that General Cermak had a dual rule, on the one hand, a military role as garrison commander; and, on the other hand, a additional role dealing with normalisation of civilian life?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you have stated, both in your statement and today, your understanding of some of General Cermak's responsibilities in Knin. Was one of these responsibilities also to keep order in the town?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I did not see Mr. Cermak's appointment in Knin as somebody who would replace the normal system of state authorities and the functioning of the bodies of state administration, which had been established, and which were performing their duties. The government's organisation was in place, and the appointment of Mr. Cermak did not suspend that. The Knin garrison was a formal and legal framework for Mr. Cermak to be sent to Knin in uniform, where he would help the normalisation of civilian life in town. That was my understanding of Mr. Cermak's appointment. I am sure that Mr. Cermak was not professionally challenged by that position, and he probably never -- I'm sure that he never wanted to pursue his career in that sense. The way I understood things was that he already had a well-established job and that his intention was not to be reactivated as a career officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radin. You will agree with me that President Tudjman and General Cermak had a better knowledge of General Cermak's specific responsibilities than you do; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I will agree. When Mr. Cermak was appointed the garrison commander, in my view, legally speaking, he had the authority of such a commander. No agreement between the president and Mr. Cermak could endanger the normal functioning of the system of state authority in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you P1144. This is a recording -- a transcript of a recording of a meeting that is dated 23 March 1999 between President Tudjman and General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S, at the bottom there's a reference to the interview that General Cermak gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. And General Cermak is discussing his interviews -- his interview. And if we turn the page in both the English and the B/C/S, the first full paragraph at the top in the English, and in the B/C/S as well, I believe, Mr. -- General Cermak says: "They asked me about Knin and all those earlier stories. What was my assignment in Knin. I told them my assignment was such and such, cooperation, with the international community, infrastructure, return, life, hospitals, this and that, et cetera." Then the president, then, adds: "Keeping order." General Cermak agrees: "Keeping order, preventing disorder, mine clearance and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radin, will you agree with me that based on this, one of the responsibilities of General Cermak in Knin was to keep order?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I think, and I will repeat what I already said in my previous answer, no arrangement between General Cermak and President Tudjman could change the existing legislative framework in Croatia. Therefore, when General Cermak was appointed garrison commander, he undertook all of the authorities, powers, and tasks of a garrison commander. The tasks of keeping order could not be defined in a new way. To clarify: By that arrangement and by that appointment of Mr. Cermak as garrison commander, the regular authorities of other bodies existing and functioning in that area did not change. If we look at the discussion between President Tudjman and Mr. Cermak, it brings me to only one conclusion and that is that the legal and constitutional order was in place. The authority was defined at the moment of appointment. Mr. Cermak could deal with other tasks. However, the other bodies authorised to pursue specific tasks were not relieved of that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, I'm not suggesting that the other bodies would be relieved of that obligation. But if President Tudjman appointed Cermak in a dual role, the one being the specific appointment as garrison commander, and then all these other responsibilities that you have indicated in your statement, and keeping order, as I have suggested, that meant that that's what President Tudjman expected General Cermak to do. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I would agree with you in full, given the precondition that that stood in General Cermak's appointment. I must remind you, however, that General Cermak was appointed only solely to the position of the Knin garrison commander. As far as I know, although my knowledge may be limited, General Cermak did not receive any other appointment from President Tudjman for some other tasks in Knin, and he did not receive any other appointments from the RH government to pursue certain tasks which otherwise fall within the domain or competence of the government. That is the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Radin, then the logical follow-up from your statement, from what you're saying, is that if Mr. Cermak had not normalised life, civilian life, and not performed any of the functions that President Tudjman gave him that went beyond those of a normal garrison commander, then President Tudjman would have no -- no remedy against him, right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean on -- by the term "legal remedy." The only legal remedy would to be relieve the garrison commander of his duties. But based on the fact that President Tudjman appointed Mr. Cermak as the garrison commander, and he told me, Go down there to Knin and help normalise the situation, that does not bring me to the conclusion that General Cermak was given authority to establish order, because, as far as I know, Mr. Cermak had no resources to do that. His appointment as the garrison commander could not increase his scope of authority, so as to include the police or anyone other. By virtue of pursuing his duties beyond the scope of the authority for a garrison commander is simply not possible. That could not be done under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm not going to belabour the point. I think -- I think -- I think you understand what I'm putting to you and I think your answer is clear in your response. I just want to touch upon one more role that was -- that has been discussed here as the responsibilities of General Cermak. And I believe you just earlier stated that you were unaware about whether one of the roles given to General Cermak was to communicate with the internationals, and the UN in particular, and in your statement you also mentioned that. I want to show you D296, which is another Presidential transcript; this time it is dated 7 August 1995. It will come up on the screen shortly. And if we go to page 20 in the English, page 41 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There's a decision, Mr. Radin, on this page about some problems with the internationals, the Danes and the Canadians. And in the middle of the page, President Tudjman says -- and I believe in the B/C/S it's the last entry at the bottom: "And another thing, tell them I appointed as commander of the Knin garrison Colonel General Cermak, a former minister, a serious man to solve these [sic] problems [sic]." Now, Mr. Radin, will you agree that your belief or your understanding as to the appointment of General Cermak to deal with the internationals is at odds with what President Tudjman said on 7 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: First of all, it is very difficult for me and almost impossible to comment two transcript sentences taken out of the context and without being aware of what was discussed before and immediately after that issue. Secondly, it is evidently clear that the president of the republic, by sending General Cermak to Knin, wanted to entrust him with certain duties and tasks which had to do with the civilian life and work. That is to say, somewhat beyond the scope of what is mentioned in the decision on appointment. You noticed well that it was only General Cermak and the president were in the room where this additional conversation took place. They are the only people who could with competence say what was discussed. However, whatever the subject of that conversation, legally speaking boils down to the decision on appointment of General Cermak as the garrison commander and to the fact that the president did not appoint Mr. Cermak to any additional positions. He did not appoint him as his special representative or a representative tasks -- tasked with a particular duty. He stayed with that decision on appointment. That is the legal framework within which I can state anything concerning what I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I just want to just clarify one thing, because have you mentioned this several times now and you have talked about General Cermak's legal authority. And your -- what I take your position to be - and correct me if I'm wrong - is that General Cermak's role, responsibilities, and any criminal responsibility he could face is based solely on the legal authority that he received based on his appointment as garrison commander and not on any other de facto authority that he may have had, based on his discussion with President Tudjman. Have I correctly understood your view?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Formally and legally speaking, when one looks at a decree on appointment, his duties and tasks are bound by that appointment. Of course, General Cermak can be held criminally liable beyond the scope of appointment alone. Criminal responsibility of a person cannot be seen solely through the prism of an appointment. But in the case of appointment and responsibilities of General Cermak in Knin, then, primarily one needs to bear in mind the decision of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, were you aware that the garrison commander is responsible for placement, order, discipline, and service in the garrison, and that all units and institutions within the garrison are subordinate to the garrison commander in matters of order, service, and discipline. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I did not. I did not busy myself with the military structure and did not analyse what a garrison commander is supposed to do. I spoke as a matter of principle about the way I saw the appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just for the Chamber and everyone's else references, I was reading from the service regulations, D32, Article 52, that we're all familiar with. There's also a discussion in Mr. Cermak's 2001 interview, at P2525, at pages 27 and 28, but I will not bother Mr. Radin with questions regarding those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, at paragraph 12 of your statement, you say: "According to my knowledge, as garrison commander, Mr. Cermak did not have the authority to command the civilian police." Now were you aware, sir, that General Cermak did in fact issue orders to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: No, was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And once again, Mr. President, the Court is familiar with these. I will not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- educate the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness says he has no knowledge of that, and I take it you were referring to documents which were signed by Mr. Cermak and which bear the title of order on which, whether these were orders or not, is quite a lot of debate on that. But since the witness has no knowledge of it, I don't think it's of any use to go through these documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, just change topics a little bit. You were working in the United States from September 1992 to January 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Between 1992 and early 1993, I was at Pittsburgh university for education. As of early 1993 until January 1995, I worked in the Croatian mission in Washington, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And as a result, would you not have any information regarding what may have been said by President Tudjman in meetings at the presidential palace during that period, right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you also were not on the Brioni island on 31 July 1995; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So you were not at the meeting that President Tudjman had with his military advisors on that day?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Would I also be correct in stating that you were not involved in any way in the planning of the Storm military operation?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier today in an answer to Mr. Kehoe's question at page 10, lines 6 to 8 of today's transcript, and let me just pull it up so I make sure I don't misquote you. You said that you were not privy to all the political discussions the president held with the various officials from his office. When President Tudjman would meet with other ministers or cabinet ministers, would you be involved in those meetings? And the reason I'm asking you is very simple. There is a few meetings I want to go through, but if you were not present in those, I don't want to bother you with it. So I want to try to get a general understanding of when you were present and when you were not present, and then we can go through these very briefly, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: There were different situations. There were certain meetings at which I was present, and I would -- sat through such meetings in entirety. There were other meetings which I did not attend. And yet another type of meetings during which I would be there for a part of the time and would, say, be sent by the president to do something else, or I had to leave because of my own duties. In any case, it varied from one meeting to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you were present at a meeting and it was taped, would your name be indicated as one of the participants?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: If I was called to that meeting, then, yes, my name would thereby. But that needn't necessarily mean that I actually attended the entire meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me just go through these very quickly, and we'll just go through the cover pages of each and then we'll go further if necessary. Were you present at a meeting between -- that the president had with Mr. Radic and others on 9 -- on 11 August, when the decision was made to pass a decree regarding the take-over of the property that the Krajina Serbs had left behind?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we could have P462 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I will further represent to you, Mr. Radin, that I -- I searched your name in the transcript and you did not appear as the speaker at any point of that -- that meeting.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask. It could so happen that by -- because of a technical error, my name does not figure among those in attendance but that, however, I took the floor later. In any case, I don't see my name here, and this is not a VONS session. If my name is not there and if I am not one of those ones taking the floor, then, in all likelihood, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one is P463. And this is a -- seems to a private meeting between President Tudjman and Mr. Radic. And, once again, you did not appear in the text of the -- of the transcript as one of the speakers. So would your answer be the same for this meeting as well, regarding your unlikelihood of attendance?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: The situation is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the last one that I want to go through is P466. It's a 30 August 1995 meeting. And if you can just confirm that your answer for that meeting regarding your attendance, or probably lack thereof, is the same?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: The answer is the same. If my name does not appear as someone taking the floor, then I probably was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am aware that the break is coming soon. I don't have -- I hope I can be done in the next 15 minutes, but depending on if there's any further questions, it may make more sense to have the break now. Or if you want me to try to complete -- there is a fairly large quote that I will deal with so it will take some time, but not too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to the three meetings for which you showed the cover pages of the transcripts of the recording, the witness testified that he doesn't see his name. If his name does not appear anywhere, that, in all likelihood, he would not have been present. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, if there are certain matters -- subject matters which you considered of importance, and I do not know whether you want to go through them from now or that you would move to another meeting, then you could perhaps briefly ask the witness if he has any recollection of a meeting held on those days, with this and this subject. Then he does not only have to rely on what he sees and what apparently is in the document, but we would also encourage him to rely on his recollection to the extent that would change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand the Chamber's guidance. I was trying to strike a balance between not going into topics if the witness was not present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: -- but I do -- I do understand ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we stay in an area of likelihood on the basis of documents without even having tried to see whether there is any recollection on the matter. And not to say that you would have to read whole portions of it, but as -- I think earlier you briefly referred to what the purpose of a meeting was or the subject matter. Perhaps if we would do the same. It may well be that the witness says, well, still doesn't trigger any recollection of being present, but then at least we have explored the matter in a more thorough way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will do so, Mr. President, and I can do it, hopefully, in the next five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would do that, and then we will have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, following the -- Mr. President's guidance, the first meeting that we discussed, that I showed the cover page, was a 9 -- was an 11 August meeting with Mr. Radic and others, when the decision was made to pass a decree regarding the property that was left behind by the Krajina Serbs. Do you remember, independently of what you have seen on the cover page, being present at that specific meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I don't recall that meeting. I do, however, recall discussions about that topic. I must put a hedge here because a lot of time has passed. But I think it was discussed towards the end of 1995 at a session of the Presidential Council. It was supposed to be a decree and later on a law on the take-over of property left behind during Operation Storm, but -- as well as pursuant to the Law on Housing Relations, under which one of the provisions states that if a tenant has tendency rights but is not using a housing unit for six months, he or she loses that right. This is what was, among others -- other things, discussed at presidential sessions about the situation of human rights and property in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I do understand that you have knowledge of these discussions generally. I'm asking you if you remember attending the meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered this question. I think that was the beginning of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The next one that I showed you was a meeting that had only Mr. Radic and the president as the -- as the participants; it was P463. And do you recall being at that meeting where, at one point, President Tudjman told Mr. Radic that Croatia should not even let 10 per cent of the Serb population return?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the last one was P466. Were you present at a 30 August meeting between President Tudjman and others, including Mr. Granic and Mr. Sarinic, where there was a discussion about Serbs who were trying to return to Croatia via Hungary?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, at paragraph 18 of your statement, which we have discussed briefly today already, there is a portion -- I mean, we talked about the basis for your understanding of the Prosecution's position. And specifically there is a portion that you disagreed with, which is that it was also intended to minimise crimes by denying or concealing them and giving false information about them. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Please, could you help me? Which part is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's in the middle of paragraph 18, and it is -- in the English it the sixth line, the end of the sentence. There's a list there and the last one is that: "The policy was to deliberately fail to report and investigate crimes, and to minimise crimes by denying or concealing them and giving false information about them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last portion, I think, is on your line 27.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. [Interpretation] "To fail to report crimes," are you referring to that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just keep that in mind while I want to show you a portion of the interview General Cermak gave the Office of the Prosecution in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have P2525 on the screen. And if we could go to page 20 to start. And Mr. President and, Mr. Radin, I apologise, but I noted yesterday that there was no B/C/S translation linked with the -- with the English transcript. There is a video and there is only the English one right now. So I will just read it into the record and then we can -- for everyone's sake so there can be interpretation, and we will try to find the translation and link it to the exhibit. If we could have page 20, yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Go to the bottom in the -- just to try to -- I know will you not get the full context of the interview but I think the question will be based on one portion. And if you want to look at other portions, please let me know, but I think it will be complete from the sake of my question. You see the questions at the beginning of line 21: "Who else were you not properly with in the military. You mention Mr. Susak, who else?" And if we go to the next page and I want to refer to the portion that starts at line 5, and I will read it: "I also had a telephone duel with General Tolj. General Tolj was in charge of political work, and the media as well, and he was also the spokesperson of the Ministry of Defence during Storm. Oftentimes in the media, in Slobodna Dalmacija and other papers, I criticised the situation, I said that things are happening and it's actually a shame, that some things are bad for Croatia and for the Croatian state. In Slobodna Dalmacija I said," this is Mr. Cermak speaking, "that some members of the Croatian military are to blame for what happened and that some of the blame must be put on [sic] military commanders because they have to check the military on the ground, and that not everything can be done that people were doing. And two days later there was an article in the newspaper where General Tolj was quoted saying that on the ground the Croatian military isn't doing anything, that these were some civilians who were dressed in military uniforms looting and burning. "And there was a huge article, my article was tiny, his was a huge article, and it said, The crimes in this area are not being committed by the Croatian military according to reports by the military police, but that this was being carried out by civilians who were dressed up, which was not true, and I called him on the telephone. I told him, You're sitting there in Zagreb, you don't even know what the situation on the ground is. And the truth is what I'm telling you, I'm telling you now such articles don't really help anybody. They're just negative, because hiding and lying won't help anybody. And I said some nasty things to him. He said, Well, don't be upset with me, you know, that there are people higher up. So, then he sent me basically. And that was the last I heard from him." Now, Mr. Radin, were you aware of this pressure from higher up that Mr. Tolj referred to, according to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't aware of that. But I can agree with the assessment that, as much as Operation Storm was brilliant in military, operational and any other term, whatever happened subsequently, was to -- was for nobody to be proud of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But you were not aware of any of these efforts to say that the crimes were committed by people dressed in uniforms, as General Cermak has mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: No, I did not have any direct information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one question of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A Dr. Radic was mentioned this morning. Can you tell the Court what his position was?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: Dr. Radic had many functions in the Croatian government, and I believe that at the time in question, in 1995, he was the vice-president of the government and the minister of defence and development, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President with regard to the -- the comment just now, Mr. Misetic says there's a translation error, if I could have him correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could ask the witness to repeat his answer beginning at page 38, line 23. He was the vice-president of the government and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the minister of reconstruction and development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apparently without even one word from me, it has been corrected, which is the way in which I like it. Mr. Kehoe, any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No further questions Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radin, you were asked whether had you attended a meeting in which, as it was -- yes? You receive now interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked about whether you attended a meeting and that meeting was referred to a meeting in which President Tudjman would have said something about how many Serbs, I think, the number of 10 per cent was mentioned, should remain after Operation Storm. Now, did you ever learn about the views of President Tudjman about the demographic composition of the population in the Krajina after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: As I worked with the late president, it was never my impression that his political agenda is directed against any national minority, any religion or ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: His obsession -- if I may. His obsession and his life project was to establish an independent and sovereign state of Croatia. The fact that one-third of the Croatian territory was occupied from the very moment Croatia became an independent state and different peace proposals that arrived with all sorts of different combinations may serve as an explanation for some of his statements or positions. When it comes to this element of his personal anti-Serb or any other kind of a position, save for the political option to preserve the Croatian state, his view was that long-term negotiations between the Serbs and the Croats were a presumption of peace in the area. I don't know how the two diverging thesis would go together, having in mind his attitudes towards all other nations and the assumption that he was anti-Serb. I don't know how the two go together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were not privy to any views of President Tudjman which would include that only a small portion of the Serbs living in the Krajina would preferably stay there?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: No, not in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you said in your answer that the fact that one-third of the Croatian territory was occupied from the very moment that Croatia became an independent state, that that could serve as an explanation for some of his statements or positions. It was rather unclear to me what statements you were referring to, what positions you were referring to. Is that in any relation to my question, or was it more of a general observation?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN RADIN
utterances.text: It was a general observation. Bearing in mind the fact that, in the Croatian media --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's -- if it is unrelated to my question, to the specific matter I raised, then I verified that the explanation is not in relation to that. I have no further questions. Have the questions triggered by the -- questions by the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- triggered any need for further questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my only issue with regard to the use of 462, I believe it is -- 463, P463, the 10 per cent issue, just by of clarity on that document, Mr. President, as opposed to this document reflecting 10 per cent in Croatia of the Serb population, a reading beginning on page 9 and 10, it reflects a discussion about a map in the small area in and around Karlovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think Mr. Hedaraly mentioned that the witness said he didn't know anything about it, he didn't attend the meeting, so we couldn't find any explanation. And then I asked him in -- I didn't go through what is in evidence in relation to this. The witness I mainly asked about the demographic situation after Operation Storm, a small portion I was talking about, that I don't think that we have to explain to the witness where he said that he had no knowledge, no specific knowledge of the views of the president on that, and that he was talking about matters which are not directly related to what would be the remaining portion. So, therefore unless there is any specific matter you would like to ask the witness on there matter or which could clarify the matter, because that's what I was asking, whether there were any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my apologies, Mr. President. My questions are not directed toward Mr. Radin and I don't really -- I don't want to keep him any longer than necessary. My question is just briefly to the Bench as opposed to the witness, because this is not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you wanted to draw our attention that careful reading of that document was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 9 and 10, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record, that we should pay specific attention to the reading of the pages 9 and 10 of P463. Mr. Radin, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. Of course, apart from what you testified in court, we also have your written statement which is in evidence as well, so even though you may not have spent that long a time in this courtroom, that doesn't mean that there's not more as it was summarised by Mr. Kay. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there's no queue of witnesses waiting, so that we will continue tomorrow to hear the testimony of the witness to be called by the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We did have the housekeeping matter of the exhibit marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have a -- I have a few matters prepared so that we could perhaps shorten the list. The first thing I would like to deal with is D1699. I think last week, Tuesday, the Prosecution indicated that it requested that one article be added to the submission and that it does not object to the admission of these documents, documents being articles from the Housing Act, Official Gazette number 51. We do understand that then this article was uploaded together with the others, and that a spreadsheet was compiled by the Prosecution and by the Defence with comments of a technical nature. We then invited the parties to agree to which of these comments should be put before the Chamber and how that should be done, and that the parties had a week to reply. I know that it's only tomorrow that the week is over, but, nevertheless, I inquire as to whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have not discussed the matter specifically but we had discussed it prior to the session quite at length. And I think the understanding was the documents would be admitted and we could just e-mail the spreadsheet to the Chamber which has both the Defence's comment as to relevance and the OTP's comment as to relevance, so we can send that later today. I will talk to Mr. Misetic. We'll make sure that everything in the spreadsheet is up to date, because there were some modifications, but we can do that later today, and I'm sure that Mr. Misetic and I can agree with that quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could also note for the record, I believe, Your Honour, you mentioned D1699 and I think the exhibit we're talking about is D1669.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to correct that, that I made a mistake there. It is 1669 and not, as I said, 1699. Now, comments on relevance, whether that should be sent just by e-mail. These are matters that may have an impact on the proceedings, so, therefore, I do not mind that it will be received by the Chamber through an e-mail, but it is a matter, I think in our three categories. It's not a purely -- of a purely technical -- practical nature. It is not just some impact but it goes to the -- it's to some extent argument. This is the relevance of this document, so, therefore, if you prefer to send by e-mail, then the e-mail should be filed at a later stage, because it is in the third category of e-mail communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just interested in consistency because we have done this now for a year and a half. In the Prosecution's case in-chief we had extremely voluminous bar table submissions of UNMO documents, UNCIVPOL documents, et cetera. My recollection is we did not file the Defence`s arguments with respect to relevance on all of those documents, so I'm just interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not always verified that. But I will certainly, together with Chamber staff, pay attention to that, because any comment, Look at this, look at that, this is relevant, that is why we are tendering it for, of course, is -- may have a direct impact on the proceedings, and therefore, we will certainly review whether the record is complete in this respect, and whether we would need more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is my understanding that the procedure to date has been as Mr. Hedaraly suggested for this exhibit, which was simply to e-mail the spreadsheets to Chambers, but if the Chamber now prefers that they be filed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- if we can go back and allow the Defence to file its comments with respect to bar table submitted by the Prosecution in its case in-chief, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, most important is that it is transparent as what the parties have brought to the attention of the Chamber, if it is not just of a practical nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It made me refresh the Bench's recollection at some point after one or -- after a few month's of trial we had a little -- an informal meeting on how to expedite proceedings, and that's when the Chamber laid out the guidance that bar table motions should be sent to the other party with its relevance. That party would then fill out a column in the spreadsheet saying whether they agreed, whether they objected, and that would then be sent to the Chamber. My understanding, as Mr. Misetic's, was that that would be then submitted to Chambers informally, but, of course, it the Chamber wants those filed, that is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a closer look at it. It is not because the Chamber would ignore if it would only be in an e-mail, but it is for the transparency of the proceedings, for those who will look into the matter at a later stage, which may be at stake. Then, moving to another which is a series of four, P2597. That's the Rule 90(H) issue, in relation to P2597, P2598 and P2599, and last one, P2600. The parties were given an opportunity to make further submissions as to the admissibility of these documents in light of the decision on P2593. The Chamber has not received any further submissions, which were due last week, Friday, and in this situation, the Chamber is about to admit these documents into evidence. Since I do not hear any further comments, P2597, P2598, P2599, and P2600 are admitted into evidence. At this moment, I have no other matters on the agenda. Then -- yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was the report of Mr. Kovacevic identified as D1676 with the corrigendum 1677, and we, if you will recollect, ran out of time on Friday, as the clock hand was getting to 2.00, and matters couldn't be finished in relation to that. Mr. Russo had asked that it be marked for identification. But I move that the documents, both of them, go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
